name: ECG 6 · Electrocardiologist
blurb: Read electrolytes, drugs, sudden-death patterns and board-level combinations.

topics.name: Electrolytes
topics.desc: Potassium, calcium and magnesium, and the order in which they change the ECG.

cards.q:
A patient with a borderline potassium level but clear hyperkalaemic ECG changes can safely wait for a repeat blood test.
True or false?
cards.a: False. The ECG is the better measure of toxicity. Any hyperkalaemic change mandates immediate attention.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.291–292

cards.q: Explain: First sign: tall, narrow, tented T
cards.a: The earliest sign, from about 5.7 mEq/L, is a tall T wave with a narrow base and a sharp peak: the tented T. It is symmetrical and best seen in the chest leads.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.231–232; Thaler ch7 p.292

cards.q: Peaked T waves are seen in II, III, aVF, I and V2–V6. Which is most likely?
cards.a:
Hyperkalaemia

Peaking across every territory points to potassium, not one occluded artery.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.292

cards.q: Peaked T waves plus a PR of 0.26 s and small, flat P waves suggest potassium of roughly
cards.a:
6–7 mEq/L

P flattening and first-degree block follow the tented T as potassium passes about 6 mEq/L.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.231–232; Thaler ch7 p.292

cards.q: Which axis makes a new wide QRS more likely to be hyperkalaemia?
cards.a:
Rightward, negative I and positive aVF

Thaler’s pearl: a wide QRS with a rightward axis suggests hyperkalaemia.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.231–232; Thaler ch7 p.292

cards.q: Put the classic hyperkalaemia sequence in order
cards.a:
Tall, tented T waves → Flat P waves and a long PR → Wide QRS merging into the T → Sine wave, then VF or asystole

T first, then atrial and AV conduction, then the QRS, then the sine wave.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.292–293; Khan ch10 p.232

cards.q: Explain: Low potassium: flat T, tall U
cards.a: Hypokalaemia: below 3.5 mEq/L the T wave shrinks. Below 3 mEq/L the U wave (a small wave after the T) grows taller than the T. ST depression joins in. Look in V2–V5.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.230; Thaler ch7 p.293–294

cards.q: Potassium 1.5 mEq/L. The ECG most likely shows
cards.a:
Merged T and U waves with a long QU

At very low potassium the U wave fuses with a shrunken T, lengthening the QU interval.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.231; Thaler ch7 p.294

cards.q: Explain: Calcium sets the length of the ST
cards.a: Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT by virtually abolishing the ST segment: the T rises abruptly off the QRS. Hypocalcaemia lengthens the QT by stretching the ST; the T wave itself stays normal.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.248; Thaler ch7 p.295

cards.q: Match each electrolyte state with its ECG
cards.a:
Hyperkalaemia: Tented T waves
Hypokalaemia: Prominent U waves
Hypercalcaemia: Short QT
Hypomagnesaemia: Long QT

Potassium shapes T and U; calcium and magnesium change the QT length.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.295, p.299

topics.name: Drugs
topics.desc: Digoxin, QT-prolonging drugs, tricyclics and the AV-node blockers.

cards.q: How does the digoxin ST depression differ from ischaemic depression?
cards.a:
It sags gradually off the R wave

Digoxin gives a gradual, asymmetric sag; ischaemia gives a more symmetric, horizontal depression.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.297; Khan ch10 p.232

cards.q:
Scooped ST depression and a short QT on digoxin mean the drug must be stopped.
True or false?
cards.a: False. That is the digoxin effect, expected at therapeutic levels. Toxicity shows as arrhythmias and blocks.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.232; Thaler ch7 p.297

cards.q: Which is NOT a feature of digoxin toxicity?
cards.a:
Bundle branch block

Khan: almost any arrhythmia or conduction defect except bundle branch block.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.298; Khan ch10 p.232

cards.q: Explain: Toxicity also blocks the AV node
cards.a: Digoxin slows conduction through the AV node. Toxic levels cause sinus bradycardia or sinus exit block, then first-degree, Wenckebach and even complete AV block.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.297–298; Khan ch10 p.232

cards.q: A patient on digoxin has atrial tachycardia with two P waves per QRS. This is
cards.a:
PAT with block

Atrial tachycardia (excitation) with 2:1 AV block (suppression) is the classic digoxin-toxic rhythm.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.298; Khan ch10 p.233

cards.q: Which antiarrhythmic needed a dose cut for a long QT in Thaler’s example?
cards.a:
Sotalol

Sotalol, a class 3 drug, lengthens the QT; the dose was reduced.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.299; Khan ch10 p.229

cards.q: Match each drug to its group
cards.a:
Erythromycin: Macrolide antibiotic
Haloperidol: Antipsychotic
Terfenadine: Non-sedating antihistamine
Citalopram: SSRI antidepressant

All four prolong the QT; the danger multiplies when they are combined.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.299–300; Khan ch10 p.229

cards.q: An amitriptyline overdose most typically adds which pair of findings?
cards.a:
Wide QRS and long QT

Tricyclics delay ventricular conduction and repolarisation.
cards.note: Khan ch4 p.106, ch10 p.229; Thaler ch7 p.300

cards.q: A patient on metoprolol has a rate of 48. The most likely cause is
cards.a:
Drug-induced sinus bradycardia

Beta-blockers are among the commonest causes of sinus bradycardia.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.128, ch7 p.298

cards.q:
Adenosine is a long-acting drug used to keep the ventricular rate down over days.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Its half-life is under 10 seconds: it briefly blocks the AV node to break re-entry.
cards.note: Thaler ch3 p.147, ch6 p.236

topics.name: The QT and sudden death
topics.desc: Long and short QT, Brugada, ARVC, HCM and screening the young athlete.

cards.q: Explain: A long QT means slow repolarisation
cards.a: A prolonged QT means the ventricles are slow to repolarise, and that sets the stage for re-entrant arrhythmias. Rough rule at 60–100 bpm: the QT should be less than half the preceding RR interval.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.228

cards.q: A patient on sotalol has a bundle branch block. What is the maximum safe QTc?
cards.a:
550 ms

Thaler: 500 ms normally, 550 ms when a bundle branch block widens the QRS.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.300–301; Khan ch10 p.228

cards.q: A 16-year-old has congenital long QT. Which advice fits?
cards.a:
Beta-blockers and no QT-prolonging drugs

Beta-blockers, avoid adrenaline bursts and QT drugs, and screen every family member.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.300

cards.q: Explain: An early beat on a long T
cards.a: Torsades de pointes usually starts when a PVC lands on the prolonged T wave. The vulnerable, slowly repolarising ventricle breaks into polymorphic VT that twists around the baseline.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.295; Khan ch11 p.294–295

cards.q: QT 320 ms. Which is NOT in the differential?
cards.a:
Hypocalcaemia

Hypocalcaemia lengthens the QT; the other three can shorten it.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.301; Khan ch10 p.230

cards.q: Name every lead with coved ST elevation
cards.a:
V1, V2

Brugada changes sit in the right precordial leads, V1–V2 here.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.310–311; Khan ch4 p.88–89

cards.q: A 32-year-old with a coved V1 pattern collapses with a fever. Best long-term protection?
cards.a:
Implantable defibrillator

An ICD is critical in Brugada syndrome; drugs do not prevent the sudden death.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.310–311; Khan ch12 p.394

cards.q: A small terminal notch after the QRS in V1 in a young man with syncope suggests
cards.a:
ARVC

The epsilon wave reflects slowed conduction through diseased right ventricular muscle.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.312; Khan ch4 p.91

cards.q: A 20-year-old rugby player has a murmur, LVH voltage and narrow deep Q waves in V5, V6 and aVF. Think of
cards.a:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Narrow dagger Q waves with LVH in a young athlete point to HCM, a leading cause of sudden death.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.305; Khan ch12 p.392

cards.q: Match each cause of sudden death to its clue
cards.a:
Brugada: Coved ST elevation V1–V2
ARVC: Epsilon wave
HCM: Dagger-like Q waves
Commotio cordis: Blow to the chest triggers VF

These are Thaler’s causes of sudden death in young people without coronary disease.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.314

topics.name: Pericardium, lungs, brain and cold
topics.desc: Pericarditis, tamponade, embolism, COPD, stroke, hypothermia and misplaced leads.

cards.q: Name the lead with ST depression and PR elevation
cards.a:
aVR

In pericarditis aVR is the mirror lead: ST down, PR up.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.225; Thaler ch7 p.302

cards.q: Put the stages of pericarditis in order
cards.a:
Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression → ST and PR back to baseline → Diffuse T-wave inversion → T waves normal again

Khan’s four stages, over days to weeks.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.225; Thaler ch7 p.302

cards.q: Which does NOT cause low QRS voltage?
cards.a:
Left ventricular hypertrophy

LVH raises voltage. The others dampen the signal reaching the skin.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.303–304; Khan ch10 p.228

cards.q: Sinus tachycardia, low voltage and alternating QRS heights in a breathless patient. Most urgent concern?
cards.a:
Cardiac tamponade

Tachycardia, low voltage and alternans together are a highly specific marker of tamponade.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.237–239; Thaler ch7 p.305

cards.q: Name every chest lead with T-wave inversion
cards.a:
V1, V2, V3, V4

Right ventricular strain inverts the T waves over the right precordium, V1–V4.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.308; Khan ch10 p.246–248

cards.q: Low voltage, right axis and peaked P waves in II. The likely background is
cards.a:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Hyperinflated lungs dampen voltage and verticalise the heart; cor pulmonale peaks the P.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.307

cards.q: Giant, wide, symmetrical T inversion and a long QT in a patient with sudden headache and confusion. Think first of
cards.a:
Subarachnoid haemorrhage

CNS catastrophes produce deep, wide T inversion and QT prolongation via autonomic effects.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.309; Khan ch10 p.229

cards.q: Explain: Hypothermia: Osborn waves, everything slow
cards.a: In hypothermia all intervals lengthen and sinus bradycardia is usual. The J point jumps up then plunges back: the Osborn (J) wave, best in V3–V4, gone on rewarming. AF is common below 32 °C; shivering artefact can mimic flutter.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.295–296; Khan ch10 p.248

cards.q: A 22-year-old a week after a viral illness has a new RBBB. Think of
cards.a:
Myocarditis

Thaler’s example: RBBB from active myocarditis after a viral infection.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.305–306, p.310; Khan ch12 p.391

cards.q: Lead I is inverted, aVR is upright and V1–V6 show normal R progression. Most likely
cards.a:
Swapped arm electrodes

Normal chest leads with mirror-image limb leads mean the arm electrodes are reversed.
cards.note: Khan ch10 p.234; Thaler ch9 p.354

topics.name: The athlete, the ward and the limits
topics.desc: Benign athletic changes, sleep apnoea, preoperative ECGs and what the ECG misses.

cards.q:
A fit, symptom-free marathon runner with sinus bradycardia at 40 and a PR of 0.24 s needs admission.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Both are benign effects of training; more than one athlete has been admitted needlessly.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.313

cards.q: A 24-year-old footballer has concave ST elevation V2–V5 with a fishhook J point and no reciprocal change. This is
cards.a:
Normal variant early repolarisation

Khan: the notched J-point fishhook without reciprocal depression is the normal variant common in young men.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.313; Khan ch5 p.123, ch12 p.394

cards.q: An obese snorer has nocturnal bradycardia and first-degree block on Holter. Next step?
cards.a:
Sleep study

Suspect sleep apnoea; diagnose with sleep monitoring and treat with weight loss or CPAP.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.315–316, ch9 p.356

cards.q:
A resting ECG reliably identifies who will have a cardiac complication during abdominal surgery.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Thaler: the resting ECG is rarely helpful; at most a stress test helps high-risk patients before high-risk surgery.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.317–318

cards.q: Chest pain, ECG equivocal. Which finding on repeat ECGs points to ischaemia?
cards.a:
ST elevation increasing over 30 minutes

Rising ST elevation over 15–60 minutes is ischaemic; J-point elevation stays the same.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.243, p.251

cards.q: Inferior STEMI and falling blood pressure after nitrates. Which extra lead first?
cards.a:
V4R

ST elevation in V4R confirms right ventricular infarction, which is preload sensitive.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.266–267; Khan ch5, ch6

cards.q: Which conduction pattern interferes least with diagnosing an infarct?
cards.a:
Right bundle branch block

RBBB delays only the right ventricle, so left ventricular infarct changes remain readable.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.276

cards.q:
A normal ECG during chest pain rules out a coronary problem.
True or false?
cards.a: False. Severe coronary disease and evolving infarcts can show normal or non-specific tracings; repeat ECGs and troponin matter.
cards.note: Khan ch12 p.396; Thaler ch6 p.243, ch7 p.308

cards.q: What does the computer interpretation lack most?
cards.a:
Clinical context

Thaler: the machine measures well but cannot see the patient clutching his chest.
cards.note: Thaler ch2 p.76; Khan ch2, ch12 p.392, p.395

topics.name: Board-level reads
topics.desc: Combination tracings: name every finding and the one that changes management.

cards.q: Explain: Irregular and wide: rhythm, then shape
cards.a: A 74-year-old with palpitations. Read the rhythm first: irregularly irregular, no P waves, so AF. Then the QRS: RSR′ in V1 and a broad S in V6, so RBBB. Two diagnoses, not one wide-complex tachycardia.
cards.note: Khan ch11 p.286, ch12 p.391

cards.q: Explain: Inferior STEMI with a slow pulse
cards.a: A 65-year-old with chest pain and a pulse of 40. Inferior ST elevation means the right coronary artery, which usually also supplies the AV node. Check every P: here they march independently of the QRS.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.258; Khan ch12 p.395–396

cards.q: Explain: Inferior ST up, V1–V3 down
cards.a: Inferior ST elevation plus ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V2 is not just reciprocal change: it is a posterior extension. V8 and V9 would show the ST elevation directly.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.265–266; Khan ch5

cards.q: Explain: LBBB with ST going the same way
cards.a: In LBBB the ST normally runs opposite to the QRS. ST elevation of at least 1 mm in a lead with a predominant R wave (concordant) strongly suggests an evolving infarct.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.276

cards.q: Explain: Capture and fusion beats prove VT
cards.a: A regular wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise. Capture or fusion beats, AV dissociation and negative precordial concordance favour VT. A typical RBBB shape with normal axis suggests SVT with aberrancy.
cards.note: Khan ch11 p.286–291; Thaler ch5 p.166–167

cards.q: Explain: Delta waves can fake an inferior MI
cards.a: A 26-year-old with a normal heart. Negative delta waves in II, III and aVF look like inferior Q waves. The short PR is the clue that this is WPW, not an old infarct.
cards.note: Thaler ch6 p.276; Khan ch12 p.391, p.395

cards.q: Explain: Wide, bizarre, peaked: think potassium
cards.a: A woman on lisinopril and trimethoprim feels unwell. Wide QRS, no visible P waves, tall T waves merging with the QRS. Before calling it a STEMI or an idioventricular rhythm, think hyperkalaemia: both drugs raise potassium.
cards.note: Thaler ch7 p.320 (case 13); Khan ch12 p.391

cards.q: Explain: RSR′ in V1: RBBB or Brugada?
cards.a: True RBBB has a broad, slurred S wave in I, V5 and V6. An RSR′ in V1–V2 without that broad S, with coved or saddle-back ST elevation, is atypical RBBB: think Brugada.
cards.note: Khan ch12 p.399, ch4 p.88; Thaler ch9 p.358

cards.q: Explain: No ST elevation, still an LAD occlusion
cards.a: Level 5’s de Winter pattern: upsloping ST depression at the J point with tall, symmetrical T waves across V1–V6. It is an acute LAD occlusion even though the ST is not raised.
cards.note: Level 5 recap

cards.q: Explain: Pain-free, but deep T in V2–V3
cards.a: A 58-year-old whose chest pain has settled. Deep, symmetrical T inversion in V2–V3 is level 5’s Wellens pattern: a critical proximal LAD stenosis. It needs urgent cardiology, not reassurance.
cards.note: Level 5 recap
